title: A Rectangle Class
oneLiner: Write your first class: a constructor that stores width and height, and three methods that use them.
keyTakeaway: The constructor stores the object's data (properties in C#, attributes on self in Python), and methods read it back from the object instead of taking it as parameters again. That's the whole point of a class: data and the code that uses it, travelling together.
explanation:
Write a class Rectangle whose constructor takes a width and a height (whole numbers, 0 or more) and stores them. Give it three methods: Area() returning width × height, Perimeter() returning 2 × (width + height), and IsSquare() returning true when width equals height. In Python the names are area, perimeter and is_square, and the constructor is __init__(self, width, height).

Each test creates a rectangle and calls all three methods: Rectangle(3, 4) should give area 12, perimeter 14 and not square, shown as [12, 14, false].

In C#, store the values in properties (public int Width { get; }) assigned in the constructor, and read them in the methods. In Python, assign self.width = width in __init__ and read self.width in the methods. Forgetting self (as the first parameter, or in front of width inside a method) is the classic first-class mistake.

visualizationSteps.message: The constructor runs once and stores width 3 and height 4 inside the new object.
Area reads the object's own width and height: 3 × 4 = 12. No parameters needed.
3 == 4 is false. A Rectangle(5, 5) would say true.

complexity.note: Storing two numbers and three arithmetic methods: constant time and space per object.
